This dazzling UK stock has been growing dividends at 35% a year! Here’s why it’s fallen 27%

This UK stock smashed the FTSE 100 last year, but has struggled in 2026. Harvey Jones examines its dividend history and share price growth potential.

Posted by
Harvey Jones ❯

I’ve had my eye on this UK-listed stock for more than a year. In 2025, it was easily the best performer on the entire FTSE 100, its shares soaring a scarcely believable 436%.

I decided it was far too late to buy and kept watching from the sidelines. Suddenly, it’s looking tempting again and I’m wondering whether it’s time to take the plunge.

Shares in gold and silver miner Fresnillo (LSE: FRES) rocketed as precious metals prices surged, with gold hitting a record $5,595 an ounce in January. Silver enjoyed a spectacular rally too, further boosting Fresnillo’s fortunes.

Fresnillo’s a precious metals powerhouse

The London-listed Mexican mining group is one of the world’s largest primary silver producers with substantial gold operations too.

In 2025, revenue climbed 30.5% to $4.56bn, while profit jumped 594% to $1.57bn. First-half 2026 results (4 August) were even stronger, with revenue up 74.7% to $3.38bn and profit hitting $1.46bn.

It’s a different story today. The gold price has fallen to $3,765, a drop of 33% from its January peak. Fresnillo shares have fallen roughly 27% this year, although they’re still up 162% over five years.

I don’t actually have any direct exposure to gold in my portfolio. I’ve always been baffled by its status as a safe haven, given that the price can be highly volatile. I’ve come to appreciate it as a portfolio diversifier, though, and would rather get exposure before prices start rising again, rather than afterwards.

I could track the price via an exchange-traded fund (ETF), but Fresnillo offers something extra: dividends. Its payouts have grown at an impressive average annual compound rate of 35% over the last five years. However, dividend growth has been wildly uneven. Payouts rose 480% in 2024 and almost 297% in 2025, but fell 66.5% in 2023 and 50.7% in 2022.

Fresnillo’s dividend policy is linked to earnings, which fluctuate with precious metals prices. It aims to distribute 33%-50% of adjusted profit, with special dividends possible when cash is plentiful. This is not a reliable income stock. Future payments could fall sharply if profits do.

Is this the moment to buy?

Gold’s latest slump reflects a stronger US dollar, which drives up the price to non-greenback buyers, and rising bond yields as interest rates climb. Gold pays no interest, so becomes less attractive when investors can earn more from cash and bonds.

The price could fall further, but if interest rates reverse, the dollar weakens or geopolitics gets more frightening, buyers could return in force.

Fresnillo trades on a price-to-earnings ratio of around 10.5, which looks good value to me. I think it’s well worth considering for investors who want long-term exposure to gold and silver, and will be happy even if the shares fall further in the short run.

I’m getting ready to drip feed money in, not to make a quick killing but to diversify my portfolio for the ultra-long term.

Investors chasing a more reliable 7% income yield might prefer to look at this FTSE 100 stock instead…
